title: The Winning of a Sword: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How King Arthur fought the Sable Knight and was badly wounded, and how Merlin carried him safely away from the battlefield._

King Arthur and Merlin rode together through the forest for a long while. At last they saw that they must be getting close to the place where the Sable Knight lived, the knight the King was so eager to find. The forest had been wild, deep and mossy until then, but now it grew thinner and more open, as though people lived nearby.

Soon they saw a fierce stream rushing through a dark and gloomy valley. A stone bridge crossed the stream. On the far side of the bridge lay a smooth, level lawn of green grass, a fine place for knights to joust. Beyond the lawn stood a tall and grim castle with smooth walls and a straight tower. It was built on the rocks so well that it seemed to be part of the stone itself. So they knew this must be the castle the page and Sir Griflet had told them about.

Halfway across the bridge hung a black shield and a brass mallet, just as the page and Sir Griflet had said. On the far side of the stream stood an apple tree, and among its leaves hung a great many shields with different emblems, just as those two had described. Some of the shields were clean and bright, and some were dirty and stained with blood. Some were whole and unbroken, and some were split as though in a fight between two knights. All of them belonged to knights whom the Sable Knight, who lived in the castle, had defeated in combat with his own hand.

“By the splendor of Paradise!” said King Arthur. “He must be a truly brave knight, to have defeated so many other knights by his strength alone. Indeed, Merlin, there must be a hundred shields hanging in that tree!”
Merlin answered him, “And you, my Lord, may be very glad if your shield is not hanging there too before the sun goes down this evening.”

“That,” said King Arthur, with a steady face, “will be as God wills. Truly, I want more than ever to test my strength against that knight. Think what honor I would win if I beat so brave a warrior as this Sable Champion seems to be, since he has beaten so many other good knights.”
Having said this, King Arthur at once urged his horse forward. As he came onto the bridge, he clearly read the challenge written in red letters beneath the shield:

Whoever Strikes This Shield
Does So At His Own Risk.

Having read the words, the King grabbed the brass mallet and hit the shield so hard that the noise bounced back. It came back from the castle’s smooth walls, from the rocks beneath them, and from the edge of the forest all around, as if twelve other shields had been struck in those places.

At the sound, the portcullis of the castle was let fall at once, and a knight came out, huge in size and dressed all in black armor. All his clothing and all the trappings of his horse were black too, so that he looked very grim and frightening. The Sable Knight crossed the smooth green meadow with a stately and dignified pace. He rode neither in haste nor slowly, but with great pride and a haughty look, as a champion should who perhaps had never yet been beaten in battle. When he reached the end of the bridge, he pulled in his reins and greeted King Arthur with great dignity, and with great arrogance too. “Ha! Sir Knight!” he said. “Why did you strike my shield after reading the words written there? I tell you that, because of your rudeness, I will now take your shield from you and hang it on that apple tree, where you see all those other shields hanging. So either hand your shield over to me without more talk, or get ready to defend it with your body. If you choose that, you will certainly suffer great pain and injury.”

“Thank you for the choice you give me,” said King Arthur. “But as for taking away my shield, I believe that will be as Heaven wills, and not as you will. Know, unkind knight, that I came here for no other purpose than to fight you, and to win back with my own body all those shields that hang on that apple tree. So get ready at once, so that I can face you, perhaps to your great disadvantage.”

“I will do that,” replied the Sable Knight. Then he turned his horse’s head and rode back some distance across the level lawn, and took his place where he thought best. King Arthur also rode out onto the lawn and took his place where he thought best.
Each knight leveled his spear and braced his shield for the charge. Then each called out to his war-horse and dug his spurs deep into its sides.

The two noble horses rushed forward like lightning, racing across the ground so fast that the earth shook and trembled beneath them as in an earthquake. The two knights met squarely in the very middle of the field and crashed together like a thunderbolt. They struck each other so hard that the spears burst into splinters all the way down to the hand guard and the broken stump. The horses staggered back from the shock, and only the great skill of the riders kept them from falling.
But with great spirit, each knight lifted his horse up with his own courage, and so finished his ride safely.

King Arthur was very amazed that he had not knocked his opponent down. As has been said, he was thought to be the best knight in all of Britain, the one most proven in deeds of arms. So he wondered at the strength and skill of this knight, who had not been thrown down by so great a blow against his defenses. When they met again in the middle of the field, King Arthur greeted the knight and spoke to him with great courtesy. He said, “Sir Knight, I do not know who you are, but I give you my word as a knight that you are the mightiest knight I have ever met in all my life. Now I ask you to get down from your horse at once. Let us fight this battle with swords and on foot, for it would be a pity to let it end this way.”

“No,” said the Sable Knight, “I will not fight this battle on foot until one of us two has been knocked down.” Then he shouted, “Ho! Ho!” in a very loud voice. At once the castle gate opened, and two tall squires came running out, dressed all in black with crimson patches. Each squire carried a great spear of ash wood, new and well seasoned, never yet strained in battle.
Each knight took a spear: King Arthur chose one and the Sable Knight took the other. Then each of them went back to the place from which he had started his charge before.

Once again each knight drove his horse forward to the attack, and once again each struck the other so squarely in the middle of his defense that the spears were splintered. Only the hand guard and the stump of each spear were left in the knight’s grip.

As before, King Arthur wanted to fight the battle out with swords on foot, but again the Sable Knight refused. He called out to those inside the castle, and two other squires came out at once with fresh new spears of ash wood. Each knight took a spear again, and when he was armed with it, each chose his place on that fair, level lawn of grass.

For the third time the two fine knights made ready and hurled themselves at one another in a furious charge. As twice before, King Arthur hit the Sable Knight dead center, and his spear burst into splinters. This time, though, the Sable Knight’s spear did not break. It held firm, and his blow landed on King Arthur’s shield with such force that the spear went straight through its middle. The girths of the King’s saddle snapped under that mighty blow, and the King and his horse were hurled backward. King Arthur might have been knocked to the ground, but he leaped clear of his saddle with extraordinary skill. So, though his horse was overthrown, he himself kept his footing and did not fall into the dust. Even so, the blow he received was so violent that for a little while he lost his senses, and everything whirled around before his eyes.

But when his sight returned, he was filled with such a fierce anger that it seemed as though all the blood in his heart rushed into his head. He saw nothing but red before his eyes. When this also passed, he saw the Sable Knight sitting on his horse not far away. King Arthur ran to him at once, caught the bridle of his horse, and cried out fiercely to the Sable Knight, “Come down, you black knight! Fight me on foot, with your sword.”

“I will not do that,” said the Sable Knight, “for, look! I have knocked you down. So hand over your shield to me, so that I may hang it on that apple tree, and go on your way as others have done before you.”

“I will not!” cried King Arthur in great passion. “I will not give up, and I will not leave, until one of us has completely beaten the other.” With that he thrust the Sable Knight’s horse backward by the bridle so hard that the other was forced to leap from his saddle to save himself from falling to the ground.

Now each knight was as furious as the other. Each drew his sword and raised his shield, and they rushed together like two wild bulls fighting. They thrust, they struck, they slashed, they parried, they struck again and again, and the sound of their blows crashing and clashing together filled the whole place with an enormous uproar. No one can fully imagine how fierce that fight was. The blows were so violent that whole pieces of armor were hacked from their bodies, and many deep and terrible wounds were given and received. The armor of each knight was stained red with the blood that ran down over it.

At last King Arthur, almost mad with rage, swung a blow so fierce that no armor could have stood against it had it landed squarely. Instead his sword snapped off at the hilt, and the blade spun up into the air in three pieces. Even so, the blow was so mighty that the Sable Knight groaned, reeled, and stumbled around in a circle like a blind man who does not know which way to go.

Soon, however, he steadied himself. King Arthur stood close by, and the Sable Knight did not realize that his enemy had no sword left to protect himself. He flung away his shield, gripped his sword with both hands, and swung it with a terrible stroke. It split King Arthur’s shield and his helmet and bit down to the bone of his skull.

King Arthur believed he had been killed. His head swam, his legs shook, and he sank to his knees. Blood and sweat mixed in the darkness of his helmet and ran down in a lather into his eyes, so that he could not see. The Sable Knight saw how badly he was hurt and shouted at him to give up and hand over his shield, since he was too badly wounded to fight on.

But King Arthur refused to yield. He caught the other knight by the sword-belt and pulled himself to his feet. Now that he had partly shaken off his daze, he wrapped both arms around the other knight and set his knee behind the Sable Knight’s thigh. He threw him to the ground so hard that the fall was astonishing to hear. The Sable Knight lay senseless for a while. King Arthur at once unlaced his helmet and saw his face. Although blood still ran down his own face in streams, he knew who it was. The knight was King Pellinore, who was named earlier in this history. He had twice made war against King Arthur. (It has already been told how King Arthur drove that other king away from the homes of men and into the forests. That is why Pellinore now lived in this poor, gloomy castle, and from it made war on every knight who came to that place.)

Now King Arthur saw who his opponent was, and he shouted, “Ha! Pellinore, is it you? Give up, for I have you completely in my power.” Then he pulled out his dagger and held its point against King Pellinore’s throat.

Meanwhile King Pellinore had mostly recovered from his fall. He saw the blood pouring from beneath his enemy’s helmet and understood that the blow he had struck must have wounded the other badly. He grabbed King Arthur’s wrist and pushed the dagger’s point away from his throat, so it no longer threatened him much.

Indeed, between his painful wound and the loss of blood, King Arthur had now grown very sick and faint, and it seemed to him that he was near death. So it was not hard for King Pellinore to heave himself up suddenly from the ground and overthrow his enemy, until King Arthur lay beneath his knees.

King Pellinore was wild with rage from the hard fight. His eyes were bloodshot like a wild boar’s, and foam, like a boar’s, clung to the beard around his mouth. He wrenched the dagger out of his enemy’s hand and at once began to unlace his helmet, meaning to kill him where he lay. But at that moment Merlin came hurrying up, crying out, “Stop! Stop! Sir Pellinore, what are you doing? Hold back your wicked hand! For the man who lies beneath you is none other than Arthur, King of this whole realm!”

King Pellinore was stunned. For a little while he said nothing. Then he shouted, “Is that what you say, old man? Then your words have sealed this man’s death. No one in all the world has ever suffered such harm and such wrongs as I have suffered from him. Look! He has taken from me my power, my kingship, my honors and my lands, and has left me only this gloomy, dismal castle in the forest to live in. Now that he is in my power, he will die at once. If for no other reason, he will die because, if I let him go free now, he will surely take revenge on me when he has recovered from all the harm he has suffered at my hands.”

Then Merlin said, “No! He will not die by your hand, for I myself will save him.” Then he lifted his staff and hit King Pellinore across the shoulders. King Pellinore dropped at once and lay face down on the ground like a man struck dead.

At this, King Arthur raised himself on his elbow and saw his enemy lying there as if dead. He cried out, “Ha! Merlin! What have you done? I am deeply sorry, for I see that with your magic arts you have killed one of the best knights in all the world.”

“Not so, my lord King!” said Merlin. “Truly, I tell you that you are much closer to death than he is. He is only asleep and will wake soon. But you are in such a state that it would take only a very little to make you die.”

And indeed King Arthur was terribly sick, even to the heart, from the painful wound he had received. It was only with great effort that Merlin could help him up onto his horse. When that was done, Merlin hung the King’s shield on the horn of the saddle. Then he led the wounded man across the bridge at once, guiding the horse by the bridle, and took him away into the forest.

Now I must tell you that in that part of the forest lived a certain hermit. He was so holy that the wild birds of the woodland would come and rest on his hand while he read his prayer book. He was so gentle and blessed that the wild does would come right to the door of his hermitage and stand there while he milked them for his meal. The hermit lived so far from the homes of people that when he rang the bell for morning or evening prayers, there was hardly ever anyone to hear it except the wild creatures nearby. Even so, royal folk and others of high rank would sometimes come to this remote and lonely place, as if on a pilgrimage, because the hermit was so very saintly.

So Merlin brought King Arthur to this sanctuary. When they arrived, he and the hermit lifted the wounded man down from his saddle, while the hermit spoke many words of pity and sorrow. Together they carried him into the holy man’s cell. There they laid him on a couch of moss, unlaced his armor, and searched his wounds. They bathed them with pure water and bandaged his hurts, for the hermit was a very skilled healer. For all that day and part of the next, King Arthur lay on the hermit’s bed like a man about to die. He saw everything around him as though through thin water. His breath hung and fluttered on his lips, and he could not even lift his head from the bed because of the weakness that lay upon him.

Now on the afternoon of the second day, a great noise and bustle broke out in that part of the forest. The Lady Guinevere of Cameliard had come on a pilgrimage to the holy man, together with her Court of ladies and knights. The fame of his saintliness had reached even the place where she lived. The lady had a favorite page who was very sick with a fever. She hoped the holy man might give her some charm or amulet that could cure him. So she had come to that place with her whole Court, and all that part of the forest was bright with fine clothing. The silence there was filled with the sound of talk and laughter, songs, the chattering of many voices, and the neighing of horses. The Lady Guinevere rode in the midst of her damsels and her Court. Her beauty outshone theirs as the morning star outshines all the lesser stars around it. Then and ever afterward, all the Courts of Chivalry held her to be the most beautiful lady in the world.

When the Lady Guinevere reached that place, she saw King Arthur’s milk-white war-horse standing near the hermitage, cropping the green grass of the open glade. She also saw Merlin standing beside the door of the cell. She asked him whose noble war-horse it was that grazed in that lonely place, and who lay inside the cell. Merlin answered her, “Lady, the one who lies within is a knight. He is so badly wounded that he is sick almost to death!”

“Heaven have pity!” cried the Lady Guinevere. “What a sad thing you tell me! Now I beg you to lead me to that knight at once so that I may see him. For I have in my Court a very skilled healer, who is well used to curing the hurts that knights receive in battle.”

So Merlin brought the lady into the cell, and there she saw King Arthur stretched out on the bed. She did not know who he was. Yet it seemed to her that in all her life she had never seen a knight of such noble appearance as the one who lay badly wounded in that lonely place. King Arthur looked up to where she stood beside his bed of pain, surrounded by her maidens. In his great weakness he did not know whether the one he saw was a mortal lady or some tall, stately angel. Perhaps she had come down from one of the lordly Courts of Paradise to visit him in his pain and trouble. The Lady Guinevere was filled with pity at the sight of King Arthur’s sorrowful state. So she called the skilled healer who was with her Court. She told him to bring a certain alabaster box of very precious balsam. She commanded him to examine the knight’s wounds and to anoint them with the balsam, so that he might be healed of his hurts as quickly as possible.

So the wise and skilled healer did as the Lady Guinevere commanded, and at once King Arthur felt all his aches fade away and his spirit grow content. When the Lady and her Court had gone, he found his heart greatly lifted. Three days later he was completely healed, and he was as well and strong and lively as he had ever been in all his life.

This was the first time King Arthur ever saw that beautiful lady, the Lady Guinevere of Cameliard. From that time on he never forgot her, and she was almost always in his thoughts. So when he had recovered, he said to himself, “I will forget that I am a king, and I will cherish the thought of this lady. I will serve her faithfully, as a good knight may serve the lady he has chosen.”
And so he did, as you will hear later in this book.
